title: Before the Pillar Boxes
passage:
Before the pillar boxes came, a letter in Draystow was handed in at a hatch beside a shop door. Shops that did the work were called receiving houses, and the keeper was allowed threepence for every hour the hatch stood open, and not a penny for the letters themselves. The quarterly returns recorded the hours and the letters. The town’s two receiving houses, a chandler’s and a bookseller’s, faced each other across the market place. In the Michaelmas quarter of 1846 the chandler’s hatch opened at seven in the morning and took in 412 letters; the bookseller’s opened at two and took in 390. Both shut when the evening cart went at eight. The surveyor’s note for that quarter remarked only that the chandler’s flap wanted a new spring.
– Clement Nabbsworth

questions.prompt: What is implied here about the two receiving houses?

options.text: The keepers stretched their opening hours in order to earn more of the hourly allowance.
The shop that kept its hatch open longer took in far more letters than the other.
The bookseller made up for much of his later start by staying open after the cart.
The cart’s hour, not the length of opening, governed how many letters a hatch took.

questions.rationale: TYPE-002, one_inch_inference off two figures the passage sets side by side and never joins. The documented facts are: (i) both shops shut when the evening cart went at eight; (ii) the chandler's hatch opened at seven in the morning, thirteen hours before that, and took in 412 letters in the quarter; (iii) the bookseller's opened at two, six hours before the cart, and took in 390; (iv) the two shops faced each other across the same market place, so they drew on one town and one trading day. Seven extra hours of opening bought about twenty-two extra letters, while the six hours the two shops shared carried nearly four hundred at each counter. The reader must supply the connection: what a hatch took in was governed by the hour the cart went, not by how long the hatch stood open - key D. Nothing in the passage states this, and no general knowledge of receiving houses supplies Draystow's two figures. A = the incentive misread, the most tempting wrong answer because the passage hands the solver a per-hour allowance and a shop open thirteen hours and invites the arithmetic of self-interest. It dies on the bookseller: the same allowance, on the same terms, bought six hours across the square. An allowance that leaves one keeper at six hours and another at thirteen is not what settled either man's hours, and the passage never says a keeper stretched anything. B = magnitude distortion, the law-11 corollary trap - a detail bent, not quoted faithfully. The direction is right (the longer hatch did take in more) and the figures are the passage's own, so a skimmer who reads 412 and works out the thirteen hours behind it takes it; but 412 against 390 is twenty-two letters, and 'far more' is exactly the word the numbers refuse. C = the compensation misread, and the option that carries the cautious surface ('much of'). A solver who has noticed that one hatch opened at seven and the other at two will look for something that evens the two shops up, and a later closing is the obvious candidate; the passage closes that door in one flat sentence - both shut when the evening cart went at eight - so the bookseller kept no hours at either end that the chandler did not also keep. C is refuted by the single fact the key rests on, which is why it sits where it does: it puts a third option on the opening-hours-and-collection-time axis, so the sheet no longer offers a bare contradictory pair (B against D) with two off-axis options beside it, and a blind solver cannot reason that the key must be one of the only two options that engage the question. Hedge balance (rules 10/13): the key D is a flat, unhedged causal assertion; the single qualified-sounding option is still C, a distractor, since the repair kept the cautious surface on it ('much of his later start'), so 'pick the moderate answer' scores zero on this sheet. No option carries a hard absolutizer from mech.py's list, so 'strip the absolutes' gets no purchase either.
